geometric.name: Geometric optics and imaging
geometric.description: Check the ray-optics basics — Snell's law, total internal reflection and the critical angle, thin-lens imaging, numerical aperture and f-number, aberrations and ABCD matrices — with multiple-choice questions that include calculations.
geometric.intro:
When the wavelength of light is much smaller than the components it meets, light can be treated as rays that travel in straight lines and bend at boundaries between materials of different refractive index. The bending is set by Snell's law, n₁ sinθ₁ = n₂ sinθ₂, and light traveling from the higher-index side is totally reflected once the angle of incidence exceeds the critical angle. Optical fibers and prisms rely on this total internal reflection.
In lens design you need the imaging equation and magnification, plus the numerical aperture NA (= n sinθ) and f-number that describe the cone of focused light, and the spherical and chromatic aberrations that degrade the image. ABCD matrices, which track a ray's height and angle with a 2×2 matrix, let you handle multi-lens systems, laser resonators and even Gaussian-beam propagation in the same form.

wave.name: Interference and diffraction
wave.description: Explore light as a wave — Young's experiment, thin-film interference and anti-reflection coatings, the Michelson interferometer, Fabry–Perot resonators, diffraction gratings and the Airy disk — with multiple-choice questions.
wave.intro:
Viewed as a wave, overlapping light reinforces or cancels depending on the phase relationship. A quarter-wave anti-reflection coating, the Michelson interferometer that measures length using the wavelength as a ruler, and the Fabry–Perot resonator that bounces light many times between mirrors to create sharp transmission peaks all rely on this interference. The range over which fringes remain visible is set by the coherence length λ²/Δλ.
Diffraction is the spreading of light by apertures and periodic structures. A circular aperture produces its first dark ring at an angle of 1.22λ/D, which sets the resolution limit of a lens. A diffraction grating separates wavelengths through d sinθ = mλ and is widely used in spectrometers and as a wavelength-selective element in optical communications.

polarization.name: Polarization and crystal optics
polarization.description: Check linear, circular and elliptical polarization, Malus's law, Brewster's angle, wave plates, birefringence, Jones matrices, and Faraday rotators and optical isolators with multiple-choice questions.
polarization.intro:
Light is a transverse wave, and the direction in which its electric field oscillates is its polarization. The amplitudes and phase difference of two orthogonal components determine whether light is linearly, circularly or elliptically polarized. The intensity through a polarizer follows Malus's law, I = I₀cos²θ, and light reflected at Brewster's angle is purely s-polarized. Jones calculus, which uses two-component vectors and 2×2 matrices, is convenient for polarization calculations.
Crystals such as calcite and quartz are birefringent — their refractive index depends on polarization — so choosing the thickness turns them into quarter-wave or half-wave plates that convert polarization. The Faraday effect, which rotates polarization in a magnetic field, is nonreciprocal: the rotation does not cancel on the return trip. That makes it essential for optical isolators that protect semiconductor lasers from back-reflections.

laser.name: Lasers and Gaussian beams
laser.description: Learn stimulated emission and population inversion, three- and four-level systems, resonator stability and longitudinal modes, the Rayleigh range and divergence of Gaussian beams, Q-switching, mode locking and M² through multiple-choice questions.
laser.intro:
A laser amplifies light by stimulated emission in a gain medium with a population inversion, and oscillates by circulating the light in a resonator formed by two mirrors. In thermal equilibrium very few atoms occupy the upper level, so pumping — typically in a four-level system — is used to create the inversion. A resonator has a stability condition set by the mirror curvatures and spacing, and its longitudinal modes are spaced by c/(2nL).
Most laser light propagates as a Gaussian beam: it stays nearly collimated within the Rayleigh range zR = πw₀²/λ of its waist radius w₀ and spreads at an angle λ/(πw₀) far away. The quality of a real beam is expressed by M². Q-switching and mode locking produce short pulses from nanoseconds down to femtoseconds with high peak power, used in laser machining and measurement.

fiber.name: Optical fibers and waveguides
fiber.description: Check numerical aperture and V-number, the single-mode condition, mode field diameter, attenuation and splice loss, chromatic dispersion and PMD, EDFAs and the basics of nonlinear effects, with multiple-choice questions that include optical-communication calculations.
fiber.intro:
An optical fiber guides light by confining it in a core whose refractive index is slightly higher than the cladding's. The acceptance angle is given by the numerical aperture NA = √(n₁² − n₂²), and the number of guided modes by V = 2πaNA/λ; the fiber is single-mode when V < 2.405. Silica fiber loss is as low as about 0.2 dB/km in the 1.55 µm band and rises at shorter wavelengths because of Rayleigh scattering.
In high-speed, long-haul transmission, pulses are broadened by chromatic dispersion — the dependence of group velocity on wavelength — and by PMD, the difference in delay between polarizations. Erbium-doped fiber amplifiers (EDFAs) amplify many wavelengths at once while the signal stays optical, which underpins wavelength-division multiplexing. At high powers, nonlinear effects such as Brillouin scattering and self-phase modulation can no longer be ignored.

detectors.name: Photodetectors and light detection
detectors.description: Check photon energy, quantum efficiency and responsivity, PIN photodiodes and APDs, shot and thermal noise, NEP, dark current, RC bandwidth and receiver sensitivity with multiple-choice questions that include numerical calculations.
detectors.intro:
A photodetector absorbs photons with energy greater than the band gap, creating electron-hole pairs that are collected as current. The photon energy is E[eV] ≈ 1240/λ[nm], so the material's band gap sets the cutoff wavelength. The current produced per watt of light is the responsivity R = ηqλ/(hc), which is proportional to wavelength when the quantum efficiency is constant.
Receiver performance is set by noise. The main sources are shot noise from the discreteness of charge, thermal noise in resistors, and dark current. An APD overcomes thermal noise with internal multiplication but adds excess noise. In fast receivers, the structure is chosen by weighing both the RC bandwidth from the junction capacitance and load resistance and the carrier transit time.

silicon-photonics.name: Silicon photonics
silicon-photonics.description: Learn the index contrast and group index of SOI waveguides, directional couplers and MMIs, the FSR and Q of ring resonators, thermo-optic phase shifters, MZM bias points and grating coupling through multiple-choice design calculations.
silicon-photonics.intro:
In silicon photonics, the roughly 220 nm silicon layer of an SOI wafer is patterned into wire waveguides about 500 nm wide, and the large index contrast with the surrounding oxide confines the light. Bend radii of a few micrometers are possible, so directional couplers and MMI splitters, Mach–Zehnder interferometers and ring resonators can be integrated in a small area. A ring's FSR is λ²/(n_gL), set by the group index.
Silicon's thermo-optic coefficient is large, about 1.8×10⁻⁴ /K, so heaters can tune phase and resonance wavelength — but temperature control is essential. Modulators use the free-carrier dispersion effect, coupling to fiber uses grating couplers or edge couplers, and germanium is added for photodetection.

measurement.name: Optical measurement and systems
measurement.description: Check measurements that use light — dBm conversion and power meters, spectrometer resolution, OTDR, LiDAR (ToF and FMCW), OCT, Doppler measurement and lock-in detection — with multiple-choice questions.
measurement.intro:
In optical measurement, the basics are to handle power in dBm and estimate loss and gain by adding decibels. A spectrometer's resolution is set by the number of grating grooves illuminated, and a linewidth narrower than an optical spectrum analyzer's resolution bandwidth cannot be measured directly. Fiber loss and the location of breaks are found with an OTDR, which measures the round-trip time of backscattered light.
For ranging there are ToF methods, which time a pulse's round trip, and FMCW methods, which derive distance and velocity from the beat of interfering frequency-swept light; both are used in LiDAR for autonomous driving. OCT exploits the short coherence length of broadband light to image cross-sections of living tissue with micrometer resolution.

nonlinear.name: Nonlinear optics
nonlinear.description: Check second-harmonic generation and phase matching, quasi-phase matching, sum-frequency generation and optical parametric oscillation, the Pockels and Kerr effects, self-phase modulation and optical solitons, with multiple-choice questions that include wavelength-conversion calculations.
nonlinear.intro:
When intense light enters a material, the polarization is no longer proportional to the electric field, and components proportional to E² and E³ appear. The second-order susceptibility χ⁽²⁾ exists only in crystals that lack inversion symmetry; it drives second-harmonic generation, which doubles the frequency, sum- and difference-frequency generation, which add and subtract the frequencies of two beams, and optical parametric processes, which split a pump into two longer-wavelength beams. Efficient conversion requires phase matching, which keeps the waves in step.
The third-order susceptibility χ⁽³⁾ is present in every material, including glass, and produces the optical Kerr effect, in which the refractive index changes in proportion to intensity: n = n₀ + n₂I. In optical fibers, self-phase modulation — phase changes driven by the time variation of intensity — broadens the spectrum, and when it balances anomalous dispersion the pulse travels unchanged as an optical soliton. This field underpins green and ultraviolet lasers, tunable sources and ultrafast pulse technology.

optical-design.name: Imaging and optical design
optical-design.description: Check the basics of lens design — aperture stops and pupils, f-number and image irradiance, the five Seidel aberrations and achromats, diffraction-limited resolution, MTF and pixel sampling, depth of field and Strehl ratio — with multiple-choice questions.
optical-design.intro:
Lens performance starts from the aperture stop that limits the light bundle and its images, the entrance and exit pupils. The f-number sets both image brightness and the size of diffraction, and each full stop down halves the irradiance. As the aperture or field angle grows, the paraxial approximation breaks down and the five Seidel aberrations appear: spherical aberration, coma, astigmatism, field curvature and distortion. Chromatic aberration is canceled by combining glasses with different Abbe numbers.
Even with aberrations well corrected, resolution is limited by diffraction to 0.61λ/NA, and depth of focus shrinks in inverse proportion to NA squared. Image quality is evaluated by the MTF, which describes how contrast is transferred at each spatial frequency, and by the Strehl ratio, the ratio of peak intensities of the point image. When pairing a lens with an image sensor, the design must also account for the pixel Nyquist frequency, aliasing and depth of field.

photometry-color.name: Photometry and color
photometry-color.description: Check the difference between radiometric and photometric quantities, luminous efficiency and lumens, candelas, lux and cd/m², the inverse-square and cosine laws for illuminance, color temperature and color rendering, and color-matching functions and the chromaticity diagram, with multiple-choice questions that include calculations.
photometry-color.intro:
Radiometric quantities measure the energy of light in watts, while photometric quantities measure it by the brightness the human eye perceives. The eye's sensitivity varies with wavelength: the photopic luminous efficiency function V(λ) peaks at 555 nm, where 1 W corresponds to 683 lm. The amount of light leaving a source is the luminous flux (lm), its strength in a given direction is the luminous intensity (cd), the density of light falling on a surface is the illuminance (lx), and the brightness of a surface is its luminance (cd/m²); the illuminance from a point source follows the inverse square of distance and the cosine of the angle of incidence.
Color can be expressed by three numbers that represent the responses of three types of cones. Weighting a light's spectrum with the CIE color-matching functions gives the tristimulus values XYZ, and the chromaticity coordinates x and y found from them place every color as a point on the chromaticity diagram. The color of a white source is expressed by its color temperature, by analogy with blackbody radiation, and how faithfully it renders the colors of illuminated objects is rated by the color rendering index Ra. These ideas are essential to the color design of lighting, displays and cameras.
photometry-color.blurb: Luminous flux, illuminance, color temperature, chromaticity

spectroscopy.name: Spectroscopy and interferometric measurement
spectroscopy.description: Learn the grating equation and the resolving power mN, blazing and reciprocal linear dispersion, prism spectroscopy, the Michelson interferometer and Fourier transform spectroscopy (FTIR), and the finesse of Fabry–Perot interferometers, with multiple-choice questions that include calculations.
spectroscopy.intro:
A spectrometer separates light by wavelength and measures its strength. With a diffraction grating, the grating equation d(sinα + sinβ) = mλ sets the diffraction angle for each wavelength, and the resolving power is limited by mN, the product of the number of illuminated grooves and the order. How far wavelengths spread out on the detector is expressed by the reciprocal linear dispersion d cosβ/(mf), which together with the slit width and pixel size determines the practical resolution. A prism has no order overlap, but its dispersion varies strongly with wavelength.
Spectroscopy can also be done with interferometers. Fourier transforming the interferogram recorded while moving the movable mirror of a Michelson interferometer gives the spectrum at all wavelengths at once, with a resolution set by the inverse of the maximum path difference. This is FTIR, widely used in infrared spectroscopy. A Fabry–Perot interferometer has a very high resolving power, the product of the finesse and the order, and is used to observe laser modes and the fine structure of spectral lines.
